chunks: One of our companions, from Ali ibn Asbaat, from Abu Makhlad al-Sarraj, who said:

I was in the presence of Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) when Muattib came to him and said, 'Two men are at the door.' He said, 'Let them in.' So they entered. One of them said, 'I am a saddler who sells tiger skins.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Are they tanned?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'There is no problem with it.'

key_terms.سَرَّاجٌ: Saddler (one who makes or sells saddles and leather goods)
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِهِ بَأْسٌ: There is no problem with it / It is permissible

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to sell tiger skins in Islam?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the practical jurisprudence of trade by Imam al-Sadiq (AS), who clarifies that the permissibility of selling tiger skins hinges on the process of tanning, which renders the raw hide pure and suitable for commercial use. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on distinguishing between the intrinsic nature of the animal and the processed state of its parts, a key principle in determining halal market transactions. The specific mention of a 'tiger' (or large cat) underscores the detailed scrutiny applied to exotic or high-value goods in early Islamic markets.
